text:
**Jacek Karpiński** was a pioneering Polish computer engineer born in 1927 in Turin, Italy, into an intellectual family with a strong scientific and mountaineering heritage. After surviving severe injuries during World War II and active participation in the Polish resistance, he pursued education in electro-mechanical sciences and graduated from Warsaw University of Technology in 1951. Karpiński made significant early contributions, including constructing the AAH (Analytical Analyzer of Harmonics) and pioneering the world’s first transistor-based differential equations analyzer, AKAT-1 (1959). Awarded a UNESCO scholarship, he visited leading US research centers, where he interacted with notable computer scientists such as Claude Shannon.
Karpiński also developed one of the first perceptrons in the world (1964) and created innovative computers including the KAR-65 and the highly advanced minicomputer K-202 (1973). The K-202 featured groundbreaking attributes like memory segmentation with paging and performance rivaling Western competitors, but despite technical success, political and industrial obstacles in communist Poland limited its production and dissemination. After losing support, he left the computing field, moving to animal husbandry, later working in Switzerland, and eventually returning to Poland. Controversies include his role as a secret informant for Polish security services during the Cold War, mostly collecting technology-related information. He was recognized posthumously with prestigious state honors and remains a symbol of ingenuity hindered by political circumstances in Poland’s history.
